you may feel some sympathy with the jews struggling to cope with 613 laws and wondering which were the important ones. but have you ever felt overwhelmed by the rules and regulations of your own tradition? and have you ever been blessed by meeting someone, or reading something, that was able to cut through all the layers and point out to you what is essential in life? who was that person? what dids/he say or do? is there some phrase or text that encapsulates such wisdom for you? 2. if you were asked what is most im- portant in life, what would your answer be? recall the experiences and relationships you have had. which are the ones that you treasure most? what has particularly enriched your life? how would you enco urage another person who asked you hows/he could live a full life? prayer your love, o god is boundless. we who were strangers have been made your children. we who were defenceless have been brought into your household. keep us mindful of your deeds of mercy, that we may love you with all our heart and love our neighbour as ourselves. we ask this through our lord jesus christ, your son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the holy spirit, god for ever and ever. amen. jesus does not pluck his summary teaching from the air— he quotes from the shema yisrael, the great daily prayer of judaism found in deuteronomy 6. the second part about the love of neighbour is taken from leviticus 18. this mission statement stands as a resounding appeal to us today. we are asked not just to believe that there is a god, but to love god. we are asked not just to respect our neighbour, but to love our neighbour. love is not only the truth about human beings but also the truth about god, who is love itself. prayer great and loving god, your love for us is beyond what we can grasp with our minds and hearts. let such great love for all awaken in us a true love of you and lead to authentic service of our neighbour.• first reading (exodus 22:20–26): god commands the israelites not to wrong or oppress aliens, widows, orphans, or the poor. he warns that he hears their cries and will act with compassion and justice toward the helpless. explore further study resources via catholic produc tions. second reading (1 thessalonians 1:5c–10): st. paul praises the thessalonians for turning away from idols to serve the living god and for living out the faith with joy through the holy spirit, becoming an example to believers everywhere. gospel (matthew 22:34–40): when tested by a pharisee about the greatest commandment, jesus summarizes the entire law and prophets into two inseparable pillars: love god with all your heart, soul, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. family of parishes meeting - wednesday 28th october 7pm in blackrock parish mon - wed. 9.00am - 12. 30pm the scripture readings today challenge us to re flect on our response to god’s commandment of love. in the first reading we hear of the loving relationship the people of israel were expected to have towards the under privileged and vulnerable. widows and orphans; people forced to le ave their countries due to circumstances such as wars, plagues or famines; as well as the poor who had to borrow to survive. the israelite people had been treated compassionately by a god of love in their times of vulnerability and now were to treat others as they themselves were treated. in the second reading, paul praises the thessalo nians for remaining faithful to the gospel in spite of obstacles. the life that they lived by the power of the holy spirit enabled them to spread their loving faith in god to surrounding places; b ecoming a model for others by the witness of their lives. we too are called to do the same. may we witness to others the joy of the gosp el both in word and deed. in the gospel, the pharisees put a question to jesus asking ‘which is the greatest commandment of the law’. in response, jesus says'you shall love the lord your god with all your heart, a nd with all your soul, and with all your mind.' this is the greatest and first commandment. and the second is like it:'you shall love your neighbour as yourself’. to love god with our whole being means having god as the centre of our life. if god is at the centre of our lives then loving our neighbour ought to flow from that. it sounds simple but it is very challenging! i’m sure we all face situations where we find it difficult to love our neighbour as ourselves - our neighbour may be someone we work with, live with - yet jesus also created th at person out of love and jesus died for that perso n. the love we know god has for ourselves is also the love god has for the person beside me, for the people i may not particularly like, and the people who may not particularly like me. if we really think about god loving everyone as much as he loves us, we’d see everyone in a new way! sick calls synodal pathway: conversation in the spirit: the synod has been an authentic spiritual experience - indeed, it would be more accurate to describe it as an experience òin the spiritó. the category of an experience in the spirit now invites us to adopt it as a key for interpreting the ecclesial processes presently underway. one of the most significant features accompanying the synodal experience of these years has been the choice of òconversation in the spiritó as its method. the effort required of everyone - indeed, of everyone - to arrive at a new awareness capable of grasping the substantial difference between spiritual conversation (as a thematic exercise) and conversation in the spirit( that is, entering into the self-giving and self - communication of the risen lord among us through the work of the spirit) has itself become a testimony to the cry of faith dwelling in òecclesiae in synodo perficiendaó (òthe church finding its fulfillment in the synodó). we desire to encounter the risen lord; we desire to experience and live concretely our identity as disciples. beyond the method itself, what struck so many participants was the discovery that ecclesial discernment consists not primarily in the exchange of opinions or confrontation of ideas, but in a shared search for what the spirit is saying to the churches today. (cardinal mario grech, secretary general of the synod of bishops, at the extraordinary consistory of bishops, convened at the vatican 26-27 june 2026). & date for your diary: alpha for adults and youth alpha will take place in blackrock parish centre commencing on 6th january 2027 - more details available soon. sacristan: ciarán ryan 30th sunday in ordinary time - 23rd / 24th october 2026 we remember in our prayer at mass this weekend the following whose anniversaries and month’s mind occur at this time: jimmy slevin michael king chris hehir michael hehir joe kelly kitty mcevoy henry leonard (month’s mind) josephine smith fidelma & jerry neville from the deacon’s desk this sunday’s readings exodus 22:20-26 & matthew 22:34-40. living the commandment of love this sunday's readings bring us to the very heart of god's law. in the first reading from exodus, god reminds his people that genuine faith is expressed not only in prayer and worship but also in the way we treat others, especially those who are vulnerable. the israelites are instructed not to oppress the stranger, exploit the poor, or neglect those in need. having experienced hardship themselves, they are called to show compassion, justice and mercy to others. in the gospel, jesus is asked which commandment is the greatest. his answer unites the whole of god's law into two inseparable commands: to love god with all our heart, soul and mind, and to love our neighbour as ourselves. love of god and love of neighbour are not separate duties but two dimensions of the one christian calling. these readings challenge us to examine how our faith is lived in everyday life. it is easy to profess belief in god; it is often more demanding to show patience, kindness and understanding to those around us. jesus reminds us that the measure of our love for god is reflected in the care, respect and compassion we show to others. in loving our neighbour, we reveal the presence of god's love in our world. deacon eric thank you to fr kevin with fr kevin’s recent departure to his new appointment in wicklow, we would like to offer parishioners an opportunity to express their gratitude for his seven and a half years of faithful service to our parish. anyone wishing to contribute to a presentation for fr kevin can do so using the envelopes available at the back of the church. these may be placed in the collection boxes or returned to the parish office. rev eric cooney coordinator of parish administration mobile:

samaritans: 116 123 free. update from victoria i had a text message recently from fr dean in victoria, to tell me that he was exhausted. apparently some initiatives in the cathedral parish (where i spent my sabbatical) succeeded beyond the staff’s wildest dreams. in september, they had a volunteers’ fair, to get more helpers on board. cards were left out one week, then the next sunday’s homily encouraged people to sign up. as a result, 75 people volunteered. these had to be vetted and steered to ministries that matched their talents. as a result, the cathedral now has five volunteer gardeners, extra flower arrangers, and numerous stewards and ushers. there’s a lot of work in organising these. last easter vigil, 15 adults were baptised. but 21 have signed up for baptism in 2027, and 19 adults seek confirmation. all 40 meet each week and learn about the catholc faith. more work for fr dean: even reporting this sounds exhausting. fr dean also reported that the youngest of his five sons has mental health issues that have brought him to hospital and caused fr dean and his wife linda endless worry. if you have a spare prayer, please remember them, and their son, as will i. fr bernard the parish office is closed until monday november 2. point to ponder : the catholic faith is built on belonging to a shared family of faith rather than walking alone. faith requires tangible loving actions rather than just passive thoughts. aughadown

reflection on today’s gospel: what does the term ‘apostle’ mean? it is someone who is sent. jesus himself was sent by the father to reveal god to the world and to redeem humanity. jesus chose twelve of his followers and they acted as his core group of collaborators. their closeness to jesus over the time of his public ministry was a preparation for their mission in life. just as jesus had been sent by the father, jesus in turn sent out his twelve disciples to make him known, initially to the jews and eventually to the whole world. in today’s gospel he tells them: ‘and as you go, proclaim that the kingdom of heaven is close at hand’ (matthew 10:7). later in that gospel we read t he great commission, jesus’ final sending out of his apost les: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the father and of the son and of the holy spirit, and teaching them to obey everything that i have commanded you. and remember, i am with you always, to the end of the age(mt 28:18-20) this commission is now the responsibility of the whole church , not just the successors of the apostles. pope francis proposed this extension of the apostolic mission to all christians as synodality. pope leo has continued this emphasis on synodality from the beginning of his papacy. what is synodality?

family of parishes newsletter our lady crowned church st joseph’s church & holy family church sunday 25th october 2026 30th sunday in ordinary time ~ year a gospel reflection the non-negotiables … have you noticed how often the term “non- negotiables” comes up in discussions lately? each side seems to set out its non- negotiables before any conversation can begin. in today’s gospel, jesus is asked which commandment matters most. his answer offers two essentials for anyone who calls themselves christian: love god and love your neighbour. these commandments belong together. they shape all that we give and receive —in our relationship with god and in our relationships with one another. simply put, life begins and ends with love. we see these two movements in the cross. through jesus, we reach upward towards god, offering our love. and with jesus, we reach outward towards the people around us, loving them as he does. these are the foundations of our lives as his disciples. take a moment this week to reflect on these movements: how do you show your love for god?how do you show your love for others? happy october bank holiday weekend family of parishes clergy team moderator & co-pp: fr charles kiely our lady crowned church, upper mayfield, cork. telephone:
